```{r data}
library(suest)
library(marginaleffects)
library(haven)
library(lme4)

ah <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/ah_si_2026.dta"))
bangladesh <- zap_labels(read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/bangladesh.dta"))
```

## Ordinary and multilevel logit

The coefficients of a multilevel logit are on a different scale than those of
an ordinary logit, so they cannot be compared directly; the marginal effects
can. The example uses wave 1 of Add Health: about 5,800 students in 132
schools. The outcome is being a current smoker. The predictors are sex, age,
race, and whether the student's mother has a college degree, plus a
school-level variable: the share of students in the school whose mother has a
college degree. The same model is fit as an ordinary logit, which ignores the
schools, and as a logit with a random intercept for the school.

```{r school-models}
ah <- subset(ah, wave == 1)
ah$school <- ah$cluster
ah <- ah[complete.cases(ah[c("smoker", "male", "age", "race", "momeduc")]), ]
ah$momcollege <- as.numeric(ah$momeduc >= 4)
ah$school_momcollege <- ave(ah$momcollege, ah$school)
ah[c("male", "race", "momcollege")] <- lapply(ah[c("male", "race", "momcollege")], factor)

ordinary <- glm(smoker ~ male + age + race + momcollege + school_momcollege,
                family = binomial("logit"), data = ah)
multilevel <- glmer(smoker ~ male + age + race + momcollege + school_momcollege +
                      (1 | school), family = binomial("logit"), data = ah)
fit_school <- suest(ordinary, multilevel, model_names = c("Ordinary", "Multilevel"))
```

`suest()` clusters the standard errors on the school. The marginal effects
average over the random intercept, so they are changes in predicted
probabilities, as after the ordinary logit. Age and the school's share of
college-educated mothers are increased by one standard deviation:

```{r school-effects}
effects_school <- avg_comparisons(fit_school,
  variables = list(male = "reference", age = sd(ah$age), race = "reference",
                   momcollege = "reference",
                   school_momcollege = sd(ah$school_momcollege)),
  newdata = ah)
effects_school
hypotheses(effects_school, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise | term + contrast)
```

**Example interpretation:** Most effects are nearly the same in the two
models. The ordinary logit gives somewhat larger effects of age and race: for
example, its Latinx-White difference is 11.2 percentage points, compared with
8.5 in the multilevel logit (the difference of 2.6 points has \(p < .01\)).

## Random-intercept logit and probit

The Bangladesh Fertility Survey: contraceptive use among about 1,900 women in
60 districts, modeled with a random-intercept logit and a random-intercept
probit.

```{r district-models}
bangladesh$urban <- factor(bangladesh$urban)

logit_re <- glmer(c_use ~ urban + age + (1 | district),
                  family = binomial("logit"), data = bangladesh, nAGQ = 5)
probit_re <- glmer(c_use ~ urban + age + (1 | district),
                   family = binomial("probit"), data = bangladesh, nAGQ = 5)
fit_district <- suest(logit_re, probit_re, model_names = c("Logit", "Probit"))

effects_district <- avg_comparisons(fit_district,
  variables = list(urban = "reference", age = 1), newdata = bangladesh)
effects_district
hypotheses(effects_district, hypothesis = difference ~ revpairwise | term + contrast)
```

**Example interpretation:** The logit and probit models give the same
marginal effects. Living in an urban area raises the probability of using
contraception by 15 percentage points in both models, and neither effect
differs across them.
